When the deep well in Barangay Talisay ran dry during the summer of last year, the barangay council looked for a solution that would not depend on the town's overstretched water district. Councilor Mylene Bautista proposed a rainwater collection program. Under her plan, each household that attended a two-hour seminar would receive a 200-liter drum fitted with a mesh filter and a tap. The seminar taught residents how to clean their roofs and gutters, how to keep mosquitoes out of the drums, and why the collected water should be boiled before drinking.

At first, only forty families signed up. Many residents doubted that rain alone could supply their needs, and some worried that the drums would become breeding grounds for dengue mosquitoes. By the end of the rainy season, however, the participating households reported that they had bought far less water from delivery trucks. Their stories spread quickly, and more than 150 families joined the second round of seminars. The council now plans to install larger tanks at the elementary school and the health center.

For years, applicants for business permits in the Municipality of Kalinaw lined up outside the municipal hall before dawn, hoping to be served before the noon break. In January, the Business Permits Office introduced an online appointment system. Applicants now choose a thirty-minute slot on the municipal website and receive a text message confirming the time. The office reports that the average waiting time has dropped from four hours to about forty minutes.

Not everyone has benefited equally. Owners of small sari-sari stores, many of them older women without smartphones, found the website hard to use. Some paid younger relatives or neighbors to book slots for them, while others simply arrived without an appointment and were asked to come back another day. After complaints reached the municipal council, the office set aside two windows every morning for walk-in clients and placed a staff member at the entrance to help applicants register on the spot.

The head of the office admits that the system is still imperfect. Still, she points out that the old line, with its long hours under the sun, was far harder on elderly applicants than any website.

Walk into almost any sari-sari store and you will find shampoo, coffee, and cooking oil sold in single-use sachets. For families who earn a daily wage, the sachet makes sense: it lets them buy only what they can afford that day, even if the price per gram is higher than that of a large bottle. Manufacturers, for their part, have built a huge market by selling in small units to millions of households.

The trouble begins after the product is used. Sachets are made of thin layers of plastic and aluminum fused together, which makes them very hard to recycle. Most end up in canals and rivers, where they block the flow of water and worsen flooding during heavy rain. Some towns have tried banning sachets outright, but store owners complain that their customers simply buy the same products in the next town.

A more promising approach may be refill stations, where customers bring their own containers and pay for exactly the amount they need. A pilot station in Barangay Malaya sells dishwashing liquid by the 50-milliliter scoop at roughly the same price per milliliter as a large bottle. Whether such stations can spread depends on whether they stay as convenient and as cheap as the sachets they hope to replace.

Every June, before the first typhoon of the season, Lola Pacing performs the same ritual. She climbs onto a wooden stool, takes down the old biscuit tin from the top of her cabinet, and checks its contents one by one: a flashlight, spare batteries, candles, a box of matches wrapped in plastic, and a small bundle of photocopied documents. Her grandchildren used to laugh at the tin. They called it her "treasure chest" and teased her for guarding matches as if they were gold.

They stopped laughing the year a strong typhoon cut the power in their town for nine days. While neighbors lined up at the only open store for candles that had already run out, Lola Pacing calmly lit her lamp and brought out the family's documents, safe and dry, for the barangay relief registration. Now it is her eldest grandson who climbs the stool each June, and the tin has grown into two plastic boxes.

Bawat purok ay binigyan ng sariling bahagi ng lupa, at ang mga residente ang nagsalitan sa pagdidilig at pag-aalis ng damo.

Hindi naging madali ang simula. Matigas at mabato ang lupa, at ilang beses na sinira ng mga ligaw na manok ang mga punla. Gayunman, sa tulong ng isang agriculturist mula sa munisipyo, natuto ang mga residente na gumawa ng compost mula sa mga tirang pagkain at tuyong dahon. Pagsapit ng ikatlong buwan, umaani na sila ng pechay, talong, at sitaw.

Ngayon, kahit tapos na ang pandemya, patuloy pa rin ang gulayan. Ang sobrang ani ay ipinagbibili sa murang halaga, at ang kinikita ay ginagamit sa pagbili ng binhi at kagamitan. Para kay Kapitana Lorna, higit pa sa pagkain ang naibigay ng proyekto: muling natutong magtulungan ang magkakapitbahay.

items.q: TELLER : BANK :: PHARMACIST : ?
items.why: A teller works in a bank, so the pair is worker : workplace. A pharmacist works in a drugstore. MEDICINE is tempting, but it is what a pharmacist handles, not where a pharmacist works.

items.q: BRICK : WALL :: THREAD : ?
items.why: Bricks are the units put together to build a wall; threads are woven together to make cloth (unit : what it makes up). NEEDLE and TAILOR use thread, and SPOOL holds thread, but none of them is made of thread.

items.q: DRIZZLE : DOWNPOUR :: BREEZE : ?
items.why: A downpour is a much stronger form of a drizzle (mild : intense). A gale is a very strong wind, the intense form of a breeze. WIND is only the general category, and CALM is the absence of wind.

items.q: SCARCE : ABUNDANT :: TIMID : ?
items.why: Scarce and abundant are opposites, so the answer must be the opposite of timid, which is bold. SHY is the trap: it is a synonym of timid, not an antonym.

items.q: FRUGAL : THRIFTY :: CANDID : ?
items.why: Frugal and thrifty mean nearly the same thing (careful with money). Candid means open and honest, so its synonym is frank. SECRETIVE is the opposite of candid, so it breaks the synonym pattern.

items.q: THERMOMETER : TEMPERATURE :: BAROMETER : ?
items.why: The pair is instrument : what it measures. A barometer measures air pressure. Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge, wind speed with an anemometer and humidity with a hygrometer. RAINFALL is tempting because barometer readings help forecast rain.

items.q: TYPHOON : FLOODING :: DROUGHT : ?
items.why: A typhoon can cause flooding, so the pair is cause : effect. A drought can cause crop failure. IRRIGATION is a response to drought, not its effect, and SUMMER is a season, not a result.

items.q: TADPOLE : FROG :: CATERPILLAR : ?
items.why: A tadpole grows into a frog (young form : adult form). A caterpillar grows into a butterfly. COCOON is the in-between stage, not the adult form.

items.q: AUTHOR : NOVEL :: COMPOSER : ?
items.why: An author creates a novel (creator : work). A composer creates a symphony. ORCHESTRA is the trap: it performs the work but is not what the composer creates.

items.q: INCUMBENT : OFFICE :: TENANT : ?
items.why: An incumbent is the person who currently holds (occupies) an office; a tenant is the person who currently occupies an apartment. LANDLORD is another person in the tenant's situation, RENT is what the tenant pays and LEASE is the contract, so none is the thing occupied.

items.q: In a certain code, ISDA is written as JTEB. Using the same rule, how is PALAY written?
items.why: Each letter moves one place forward in the alphabet: I→J, S→T, D→E, A→B. So P→Q, A→B, L→M, A→B, Y→Z, giving QBMBZ. OZKZX moves each letter backward, and QBMBY forgets to shift the last letter.

items.q: What comes next in the series? AZ, BY, CX, DW, ___
items.why: The first letters move forward (A, B, C, D, E) while the second letters move backward from Z (Z, Y, X, W, V). The next pair is EV. EW repeats W instead of moving back one more letter.

items.q: Each letter is replaced by its position in the alphabet (A = 1, B = 2, ..., Z = 26) and the numbers are added. Under this rule, BAHAY = 2 + 1 + 8 + 1 + 25 = 37. What is the value of KUBO?
items.why: K = 11, U = 21, B = 2, O = 15, and 11 + 21 + 2 + 15 = 49. Miscounting U as 20 gives 48, and miscounting O as 16 gives 50.

items.q: All barangay health workers are trained in first aid. Some volunteers are barangay health workers. Which conclusion must be true?
choices: All volunteers are trained in first aid.
Everyone trained in first aid is a barangay health worker.
Some volunteers are trained in first aid.
Some barangay health workers are not volunteers.
items.why: The volunteers who are barangay health workers must be trained in first aid, so at least some volunteers are trained. "All volunteers" goes too far, and the first statement cannot be reversed. Whether some health workers are not volunteers is not stated either way.

items.q: No reptiles have feathers. All snakes are reptiles. Which conclusion must be true?
choices: All animals without feathers are reptiles.
items.why: Every snake is a reptile and no reptile has feathers, so no snake has feathers. "Some reptiles are not snakes" is true in real life, but it does not follow from the two statements given.

items.q: Some clerks are typists. Some typists are drivers. Which statement must be true?
items.why: "Some clerks are typists" means at least one person is both, so that person is a typist who is a clerk. "Some clerks are drivers" is the trap: the typists who drive may be different people from the typists who are clerks, so neither it nor its opposite is certain.

items.q: If it rains, the fiesta program will be moved to the covered court. The fiesta program was not moved to the covered court. Which must be true?
choices: The covered court was already full.
items.why: Rain always leads to the move. Since the move did not happen, it could not have rained (if P then Q; not Q, so not P). The other choices add facts that the statements do not give.

items.q: Office rule: If an employee is late three or more times in a month, the HR unit issues a memo. Rina received a memo from the HR unit this month. Which statement is correct?
choices: Rina was late at least three times this month.
The facts given do not show whether Rina was late three or more times.
Rina was never late this month.
The HR unit issues memos only for tardiness.
items.why: The rule says lateness leads to a memo, not that a memo comes only from lateness; Rina may have received a memo for another reason. Concluding that she was late three times is the classic error of reversing an if-then statement.

items.q: If @ means +, # means ×, $ means −, and & means ÷, what is the value of 18 & 3 # 4 $ 5 @ 2?
items.why: Replace the symbols: 18 ÷ 3 × 4 − 5 + 2. Do ÷ and × left to right: 18 ÷ 3 = 6, then 6 × 4 = 24. Then 24 − 5 + 2 = 21. Computing 24 − (5 + 2) = 17 is the common slip, and doing 3 × 4 first gives −1.5.

items.q: Notice from the Municipal Health Office: "Free measles vaccination for children aged 1 to 5 will be held on Saturday at the covered court. Parents are asked to bring their child's immunization card." Which assumption is implicit in the notice?
choices: Measles vaccines are costly in private clinics.
No child in the town has been vaccinated against measles.
Most parents of young children in the town have an immunization card for their child.
The covered court is the largest venue in town.
items.why: Asking parents to bring the card only makes sense if parents generally have one. The notice works whether or not private vaccines are costly or the court is the largest venue, and a vaccination drive does not assume that no child has ever been vaccinated.

items.q: Advertisement: "Choose Tibay rubber slippers. They last twice as long as ordinary slippers." Which assumption does the advertisement make?
choices: Tibay slippers are the cheapest on the market.
Buyers care about how long their slippers last.
Most buyers already own Tibay slippers.
Ordinary slippers break within a month.
items.why: The ad tries to win buyers with durability, so it takes for granted that buyers value durability. It says nothing about price, current ownership or a specific lifespan of ordinary slippers.

items.q: The barangay council decided to install solar-powered streetlights along Purok 4 to reduce accidents at night. Which assumption underlies the decision?
choices: Solar-powered lights are cheaper than any other streetlight.
All accidents in the barangay happen at night.
Purok 4 has no electric power lines.
Poor lighting along Purok 4 contributes to accidents at night.
items.why: Adding lights can only reduce night accidents if darkness is part of the cause, so the council assumes poor lighting contributes to them. The choice of solar power does not require it to be the cheapest option or that the area has no power lines.

items.q: Every employee of the provincial assessor's office must complete 40 hours of training each year. Dario, an employee of that office, has completed 32 hours so far this year. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Dario will be dismissed from service.
All of Dario's co-workers have completed 40 hours.
Dario must still complete at least 8 more hours of training this year.
The training is given in five 8-hour days.
items.why: The requirement is 40 hours and Dario has 32, so he needs at least 40 − 32 = 8 more hours. Nothing is said about penalties, about his co-workers or about how the training is scheduled.

items.q: Records of the rural health unit of San Roque show that, for three straight years, dengue cases rose in the weeks after periods of heavy rain. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: In San Roque, dengue cases tend to rise after heavy rain.
Heavy rain by itself causes dengue.
Dengue cases in San Roque will double next year.
The rural health unit failed to control dengue.
items.why: A pattern repeated over three years supports a tendency. It does not prove that rain itself causes the disease (rain creates breeding sites for the mosquitoes that carry it), it does not predict exact numbers, and it says nothing about the health unit's performance.

items.q: To shorten the long lines at its windows, the city treasurer's office will now let taxpayers pay real property tax online. Which assumption is the plan based on?
choices: A good number of taxpayers are able to pay online.
The office will close all its payment windows.
Most taxpayers prefer to pay in cash at the office.
items.why: The lines get shorter only if enough taxpayers actually switch to paying online, so the plan assumes many of them can. It does not need online payment to be error-free or the windows to close. A strong preference for paying in cash would work against the plan, so it is not an assumption of it.

items.q: All applicants who passed the written test were invited to an interview. Some of those interviewed were hired. Liza, an applicant, was not invited to an interview. Which conclusion must be true?
choices: Liza was hired without an interview.
Everyone who was interviewed was hired.
Liza did not pass the written test.
Liza passed the written test but did not reply to the invitation.
items.why: Passing always led to an invitation. Liza was not invited, so she could not have passed (if P then Q; not Q, so not P). The statements give no basis for her being hired, and "some were hired" does not mean all were.

items.q:
Statement: Since a new jeepney route opened in March, the usual travel time from Barangay Malinao to the town proper has dropped from 50 minutes to 30 minutes.
Conclusion I: Travelers from Malinao now reach the town proper faster than before March.
Conclusion II: Every resident of Malinao now rides a jeepney to the town proper.
Which of the following is correct?
items.why: Conclusion I restates what the travel times show: 30 minutes is faster than 50 minutes. Conclusion II goes beyond the statement, which says nothing about how many residents ride jeepneys. So only conclusion I follows.

items.q: How many sacks of rice in all did the cooperative sell from January to June?
items.why: Regular milled: 120 + 110 + 135 + 150 + 140 + 125 = 780. Well-milled: 80 + 90 + 75 + 100 + 110 + 95 = 550. Total: 780 + 550 = 1,330 sacks. 780 is only the regular-milled total.

items.q: In which month was the difference between regular-milled and well-milled sales the greatest?
items.why: Differences: Jan 40, Feb 20, Mar 60, Apr 50, May 30, Jun 30. March has the greatest gap (135 − 75 = 60). April is tempting because it has the highest regular-milled sales, but its gap is only 50.

items.q: By what percent did the cooperative's total rice sales increase from February to April?
items.why: February total: 110 + 90 = 200 sacks. April total: 150 + 100 = 250 sacks. Increase: 50 ÷ 200 = 25%. Dividing by the April total (50 ÷ 250 = 20%) uses the wrong base, and about 36% is the increase for regular-milled rice only (40 ÷ 110).

items.q: In May, what percent of the cooperative's total sales was well-milled rice?
items.why: May total: 140 + 110 = 250 sacks. Well-milled share: 110 ÷ 250 = 44%. 56% is the regular-milled share, about 79% compares well-milled with regular-milled (110 ÷ 140) instead of with the total, and 20% is May's share of all well-milled sales in six months (110 ÷ 550).

items.q: What percent of the total population of Barangay Liwanag is aged 60 and above?
items.why: Total population: males 620 + 540 + 700 + 140 = 2,000 and females 580 + 560 + 680 + 180 = 2,000, so 4,000 in all. Aged 60 and above: 140 + 180 = 320, and 320 ÷ 4,000 = 8%. 16% divides by only 2,000, while 7% and 9% are the male and female shares within their own sex.

items.q: Among residents aged 60 and above, what is the ratio of females to males?
items.why: Females 180 and males 140, so 180 : 140 = 9 : 7 after dividing both by 20. 7 : 9 reverses the order asked, and 9 : 16 compares females with the whole age group (180 : 320).

items.q: The barangay plans to give a ₱1,500 cash gift to every resident aged 60 and above. How much will it need in all?
items.why: There are 140 + 180 = 320 residents aged 60 and above, and 320 × ₱1,500 = ₱480,000. ₱270,000 covers only the females (180 × ₱1,500) and ₱210,000 only the males.

items.q: What percent of the female population of Barangay Liwanag is aged 30 to 59?
items.why: Total females: 580 + 560 + 680 + 180 = 2,000. Females aged 30 to 59: 680, and 680 ÷ 2,000 = 34%. 17% divides by the whole population (4,000), 35% uses the male figure (700), and about 49% divides by the whole 30 to 59 group (1,380).

items.q: Which name should be filed FIRST in alphabetical order?
items.why: Rule applied: file by surname first, comparing letter by letter. All four surnames begin with RAM; the fourth letter decides: Ram-A (Rama) comes before Ram-I (Ramil, Ramirez) and Ram-O (Ramos). Do not be misled by the given names: Ana in "Ramirez, Ana L." does not matter because the surnames already differ.

items.q: Which entry comes first when these names are filed alphabetically?
items.why: Rule applied: "nothing before something." Comparing unit by unit, the surname Lim is shorter than Limbo, so every Lim comes before Limbo even though Arnel starts with A. Among the Lim entries, Pat ends before Patricia and Patricio, so the shorter given name is filed first.

items.q: A surname prefix (de, del, dela, delos) is joined to the surname and filed as one unit, ignoring the space. If the four names below are arranged alphabetically, which one is THIRD?
items.why: Joined as one unit, the surnames read DELACRUZ, DELEON, DELOSSANTOS and DELROSARIO. The fourth letter decides: A, E, O, R. The order is Dela Cruz, De Leon, Delos Santos, Del Rosario, so Delos Santos is third. The trap is treating "Del" or "De" as a separate word, which would wrongly move Del Rosario ahead.

items.q: The prefixes Mac and Mc are filed exactly as written (Mc is NOT treated as if it were spelled Mac). Which name is filed LAST?
items.why: Filed as written, the second letters are A, A, A and C: MABINI, MACARAEG and MADRIGAL all have A as the second letter, while MCDONALD has C, so McDonald goes last. If you wrongly read Mc as Mac, McDonald would sit between Macaraeg and Madrigal, and Madrigal would look like the last name.

items.q: Arrange the names alphabetically. A suffix such as Jr. is the last indexing unit, after the middle initial. Which name is THIRD?
items.why: Units are compared in order: surname, given name, middle initial, then suffix. Rafael comes before Rafaela (nothing before something), so the three Rafael entries come first: A., then B., then B., Jr. (a name with no suffix comes before the same name with a suffix). Rafaela C. is last. The third name is "Santos, Rafael B., Jr."

items.q: A hyphenated compound surname is filed as one unit, with the hyphen ignored. Which name is filed LAST?
items.why: The surname Garcia-Lopez is read as one unit, GARCIALOPEZ, which is longer than GARCIA. Since the surname is compared before the given name, every plain Garcia (Ben, Mario, Zeny) comes first, and Garcia-Lopez comes last. The trap is choosing Garcia, Zeny because Z is late in the alphabet, or filing Garcia-Lopez first because of the given name Ana.

items.q: In a Filipino name, the middle name is usually the mother's maiden surname. An employee signs her name as "Rosalinda Bautista Dimaculangan," where Bautista is her middle name. How should her name be indexed for filing?
items.why: Personal names are indexed surname first, then given name, then middle name. Her surname is Dimaculangan, so the index form is "Dimaculangan, Rosalinda Bautista." Filing under Bautista is the common trap, because the middle name comes before the surname when the name is written in normal order.

items.q: Agency names are filed as written, word by word. Which agency is filed FIRST?
choices: Department of Social Welfare and Development
items.why: The first two words, "Department of," are the same for all four, so the third word decides. Agrarian and Agriculture both begin with AGR; the fourth letter is A in Agrarian and I in Agriculture, so Agrarian Reform comes first. Agriculture is the tempting choice because it is the more familiar word.

items.q: Agency names are filed as written, word by word. If these four are arranged alphabetically, which one is THIRD?
items.why: "Bureau of" is the same for all, so compare the third word: Customs, Fire, Immigration, Internal. Immigration and Internal both start with I; the second letter is M versus N, and M comes first. The order is Customs, Fire Protection, Immigration, Internal Revenue, so Immigration is third.

items.q: Case folders are filed in ascending numeric order of their file numbers (year, then serial number). Which folder is SECOND?
items.why: Compare the year first, then the serial number. 2024-0814 has the earliest year, so it is first even though 0814 is a large serial. The 2025 folders follow by serial: 0148, 0418, 0841. The second folder is 2025-0148. The trap is sorting by the serial number alone.

items.q: Barangay resolutions are filed in chronological order, earliest date first. Which date is THIRD?
items.why: Chronological filing compares the year first, then the month, then the day. The order is May 3, 2024; November 12, 2024; January 30, 2025; March 5, 2025. The third is January 30, 2025. The trap is sorting by month name only, which would put January first regardless of the year.

items.q: In which drawer should the folder of "Corpuz, Jaime R." be placed?
items.why: A drawer label gives the first three letters of the surnames inside, so every surname beginning with COR belongs in the drawer that ends with "Cor." Corpuz starts with COR, so it goes in Drawer 1. The trap is thinking Corpuz is "past" Cor and moving it to Drawer 2, which starts at COS.

items.q: In which drawer should the folder of "de Guzman, Carlo P." be placed?
items.why: Because the prefix is part of the surname as written, the filing surname is DEGUZMAN, whose first three letters are DEG. DEG falls between Cos and Fer, so the folder goes in Drawer 2. The trap is filing under G for Guzman, which would wrongly send it to Drawer 3.

items.q: In which drawer should the folder of "Linsangan, Paolo M." be placed?
items.why: The first three letters of Linsangan are LIN. Drawer 3 ends at Lim and Drawer 4 starts at Lin, so Linsangan goes in Drawer 4. The trap is Drawer 3: LIM and LIN differ only in the third letter, and N comes after M.

items.q: Which list shows the names in correct alphabetical order?
choices: Nava, Rodel; Navales, Cora; Navarrete, Joy; Navarro, Liza
Nava, Rodel; Navales, Cora; Navarro, Liza; Navarrete, Joy
Navales, Cora; Nava, Rodel; Navarrete, Joy; Navarro, Liza
Nava, Rodel; Navarrete, Joy; Navales, Cora; Navarro, Liza
items.why: Compare surnames letter by letter. Nava is shortest, so it comes first (nothing before something). Navales and Navarrete differ at the fifth letter, L before R. Navarrete and Navarro differ at the seventh letter, E before O. So the order is Nava, Navales, Navarrete, Navarro.

items.q: Choose the correctly spelled word: "The session hall can ______ up to 200 participants."
items.why: Accommodate has a double C and a double M. The most common error is "accomodate," which drops one M; a handy memory aid is that the word is big enough to accommodate two Cs and two Ms.

items.q: Which word is spelled correctly?
items.why: Liaison (a person who links two offices) has an I on both sides of the A: li-A-I-son. "Liason" is the usual trap; it leaves out the second I.

items.q: Which word is MISSPELLED?
items.why: The correct spelling is commitment: double M, single T. The final T of commit is doubled only before a suffix that starts with a vowel (committed, committing, committee), not before -ment. The misspelling swaps the doubled letters.

items.q: Choose the correctly spelled word: "The building ______ crew checks the generator every Friday."
items.why: Maintenance is spelled main-TEN-ance. Although it comes from the verb maintain, the AI of maintain is not kept: the noun uses -ten-, and it ends in -ance. "Maintainance" is the trap for people who copy the verb.

items.q: Which spelling is correct for the noun meaning "an event or incident"?
items.why: Occurrence has a double C, a double R and ends in -ence. The R of occur is doubled before a vowel suffix because the stress falls on the last syllable (oc-CUR), the same as in occurred and occurring. "Occurence" with one R is the usual error.

items.q: Choose the correctly spelled word: "Please put the original and the photocopy in ______ envelopes."
items.why: Separate is spelled sep-A-rate, with A after the P. The common trap is "seperate," because the unstressed vowel sounds like E. A memory aid: there is "a rat" in sep-a-rat-e.

items.q: Which spelling is correct for the word meaning "a system of administration run by many offices and officials"?
items.why: Bureaucracy is built from bureau (B-U-R-E-A-U) plus -cracy. Keep every letter of bureau: bureau-cracy. "Beaurocracy" reverses the vowels after B, and "bureacracy" drops the U at the end of bureau.

items.q: One word in this list of local government terms is misspelled. Which one?
items.why: The correct spelling is reimbursement. The silent E at the end of reimburse is kept before a suffix that begins with a consonant, such as -ment (as in management and requirement). The other three words are spelled correctly.

items.q: Choose the correctly spelled word: "Each applicant must answer the attached ______."
items.why: Questionnaire has a double N and ends in -aire (from French). The usual error is "questionaire" with one N; "questionairre" moves the doubling to the R by mistake.

items.q: Which of these words is spelled INCORRECTLY?
items.why: The correct spelling is embarrass, with a double R and a double S. Many writers double only the S. The other words are correct: necessary (one C, double S), receive (E before I after C) and calendar (ends in -ar).

items.q: Choose the correctly spelled word: "Only authorized ______ may enter the records room."
items.why: Personnel (the employees of an office) has a double N and a single L, with the stress on the last syllable: per-son-NEL. Do not confuse it with personal (private, of a person), which has one N and ends in -al.

items.q: Which word in this list of office terms is spelled wrong?
items.why: The correct spelling is consensus, with an S after CON. It is related to consent, not to census, which is why many people wrongly write "concensus." The other three words are spelled correctly.

items.q: Choose the correctly spelled word: "Using the office vehicle is a ______, not a right."
items.why: Privilege is spelled priv-I-leg-E, with I then E, and it has no D. "Priviledge" is the classic trap, made by mixing it up with words like knowledge.

items.q: Find the misspelled word.
items.why: The correct spelling is harass: one R and a double S. It is often confused with embarrass, which does have a double R. The other words are correct, including the silent P in receipt.

items.q: Choose the correctly spelled word: "A valid ID is ______ for claiming the cash assistance."
items.why: Indispensable ends in -able, not -ible: in-DIS-pens-able, like dispensable. "Indispensible" is the most tempting wrong choice because -ible and -able sound the same in speech.

items.q: Under the 1987 Constitution, in whom does sovereignty reside?
choices: In the President as head of state
In Congress as the representative body
In the Supreme Court as final interpreter of the Constitution
items.why: Art. II, Sec. 1 states: 'The Philippines is a democratic and republican State. Sovereignty resides in the people and all government authority emanates from them.' The branches of government only exercise authority that comes from the people.

items.q: Under Article I of the 1987 Constitution, the waters around, between, and connecting the islands of the archipelago, regardless of their breadth and dimensions, form part of which of the following?
choices: The internal waters of the Philippines
items.why: Art. I ends with: 'The waters around, between, and connecting the islands of the archipelago, regardless of their breadth and dimensions, form part of the internal waters of the Philippines.' The territorial sea is listed separately in Art. I as one of the domains, so it is a tempting but wrong choice.

items.q: Police officers, without any court order and without any law allowing it, opened and copied the private letters of a suspect. What does the Bill of Rights say about using the copied letters as evidence?
choices: They are inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding
They may be used if they prove the guilt of the suspect
They may be used in administrative cases but not in criminal cases
They may be used if the suspect does not object within 15 days
items.why: Art. III, Sec. 3 makes the privacy of communication and correspondence inviolable 'except upon lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law', and adds: 'Any evidence obtained in violation of this or the preceding section shall be inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding.' The usefulness of the evidence does not cure the violation.

items.q: A person under investigation for an offense wants to give up his right to remain silent and his right to counsel. Under Art. III, Sec. 12 of the 1987 Constitution, how may these rights be waived?
choices: In writing, before any barangay official
They can never be waived under any circumstance
In writing and in the presence of counsel
items.why: Art. III, Sec. 12 states: 'These rights cannot be waived except in writing and in the presence of counsel.' Both conditions are required. The choice saying they can never be waived is wrong because the Constitution allows a waiver that meets both conditions.

items.q: Which statement about the right to bail is correct under Art. III, Sec. 13 of the 1987 Constitution?
choices: The right to bail shall not be impaired even when the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus is suspended
All persons charged with any offense are bailable before conviction, without exception
Excessive bail may be required for serious offenses
The right to bail is automatically suspended when martial law is declared
items.why: Art. III, Sec. 13 states: 'The right to bail shall not be impaired even when the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus is suspended. Excessive bail shall not be required.' Bail is not absolute: persons charged with offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua when evidence of guilt is strong are excepted.

items.q: Maricel, a Filipino citizen, married a foreign national. Under the 1987 Constitution, what is the effect of the marriage on her Philippine citizenship?
choices: She automatically loses it on the day of the marriage
She keeps it only if her husband becomes a naturalized Filipino
She retains it, unless by her act or omission she is deemed, under the law, to have renounced it
She must elect Philippine citizenship again within one year
items.why: Art. IV, Sec. 4 states: 'Citizens of the Philippines who marry aliens shall retain their citizenship, unless by their act or omission they are deemed, under the law to have renounced it.' Marriage to a foreigner does not by itself cause loss of citizenship.

items.q: Which set of qualifications for voting is found in Art. V, Sec. 1 of the 1987 Constitution?
choices: At least 18 years old, a resident of the Philippines for at least one year, and of the place of voting for at least six months immediately preceding the election
At least 18 years old, able to read and write, and a resident of the place of voting for at least one year
At least 21 years old, a resident of the Philippines for at least six months, and an owner of property in the place of voting
At least 18 years old and a resident of the place of voting for at least three months
items.why: Art. V, Sec. 1 grants suffrage to citizens not otherwise disqualified by law 'who are at least eighteen years of age, and who shall have resided in the Philippines for at least one year and in the place wherein they propose to vote, for at least six months immediately preceding the election.' It also says: 'No literacy, property, or other substantive requirement shall be imposed', which rules out the choices on reading and property.

items.q: What is the term of office of a Senator, and how many consecutive terms may a Senator serve?
choices: Three years; not more than three consecutive terms
Four years; not more than two consecutive terms
Six years; not more than two consecutive terms
items.why: Art. VI, Sec. 4: 'The term of office of the Senators shall be six years... No Senator shall serve for more than two consecutive terms.' Three years and three consecutive terms apply to Members of the House of Representatives (Art. VI, Sec. 7).

items.q: Under the 1987 Constitution, which bills must originate exclusively in the House of Representatives?
choices: Bills declaring the existence of a state of war
Appropriation, revenue or tariff bills, bills authorizing increase of the public debt, bills of local application, and private bills
Bills concurring in treaties and international agreements
items.why: Art. VI, Sec. 24 lists 'All appropriation, revenue or tariff bills, bills authorizing increase of the public debt, bills of local application, and private bills' as bills that 'shall originate exclusively in the House of Representatives, but the Senate may propose or concur with amendments.' Treaties need the concurrence of the Senate (Art. VII, Sec. 21), not origination in the House.

items.q: A Vice-President succeeded to the Presidency and served as President for four years and six months. Under Art. VII, Sec. 4, may that person later run for President?
choices: Yes, because the person was never elected as President
Yes, but only after a gap of one full term
No, unless Congress allows it by a two-thirds vote
No, because a person who has succeeded as President and served for more than four years is not qualified for election to the same office at any time
items.why: Art. VII, Sec. 4 states: 'No person who has succeeded as President and has served as such for more than four years shall be qualified for election to the same office at any time.' Four years and six months is more than four years, so the bar applies even though the person was not elected President.

items.q: In case of invasion or rebellion, when public safety requires it, for how long may the President place the Philippines under martial law, and within what time must the President report to Congress?
choices: Not exceeding 30 days; report within 24 hours
Not exceeding 60 days; report within 48 hours
Not exceeding 90 days; report within 72 hours
Until the rebellion ends; report within one week
items.why: Art. VII, Sec. 18 allows the President, 'for a period not exceeding sixty days', to suspend the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus or declare martial law, and requires a report to Congress 'Within forty-eight hours'. The 24-hour period in the same section is the time for Congress to convene if not in session.

items.q: How is the Commission on Human Rights composed under Art. XIII, Sec. 17 of the 1987 Constitution?
choices: A Chairman and two Commissioners, all of whom must be lawyers
A Chairman and six Commissioners, a majority of whom must be lawyers
A Chairman and four Members who must be natural-born citizens, a majority of whom shall be members of the Bar
Five Members appointed by the Supreme Court
items.why: Art. XIII, Sec. 17 provides that the Commission on Human Rights 'shall be composed of a Chairman and four Members who must be natural-born citizens of the Philippines and a majority of whom shall be members of the Bar.' A Chairman and two Commissioners describes the CSC and COA; a Chairman and six Commissioners describes the COMELEC.

items.q: How is the Supreme Court composed under the 1987 Constitution?
choices: A Chief Justice and twelve Associate Justices
A Chief Justice and fourteen Associate Justices
A Chief Justice and fifteen Associate Justices
A Chief Justice and ten Associate Justices
items.why: Art. VIII, Sec. 4(1) states: 'The Supreme Court shall be composed of a Chief Justice and fourteen Associate Justices.' It may sit en banc or in divisions of three, five, or seven Members, for a total of fifteen Members.

items.q: Under Art. IX-B of the 1987 Constitution, who compose the Civil Service Commission?
choices: The heads of all executive departments
items.why: Art. IX-B, Sec. 1(1): the civil service 'shall be administered by the Civil Service Commission composed of a Chairman and two Commissioners' who must be natural-born citizens, at least 35 years old at appointment, with proven capacity for public administration. A Chairman and six Commissioners is the COMELEC (Art. IX-C, Sec. 1).

items.q: A Commissioner of the Civil Service Commission resigned three years into a seven-year term. If someone is appointed to fill the vacancy, how long will the new appointee serve?
choices: A full seven-year term, with one possible reappointment
A full seven-year term without reappointment
Only for the unexpired term of the predecessor
items.why: Art. IX-B, Sec. 1(2) sets a term of 'seven years without reappointment' and adds: 'Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired term of the predecessor.' The trap is giving the new appointee a fresh seven-year term.

items.q: Appointments in the civil service are made according to merit and fitness, determined as far as practicable by competitive examination. Which positions does the Constitution expressly except from the competitive examination?
choices: Positions in government-owned or controlled corporations with original charters
Positions which are policy-determining, primarily confidential, or highly technical
All positions in local government units
All positions in the first level of the career service
items.why: Art. IX-B, Sec. 2(2): appointments are made 'only according to merit and fitness to be determined, as far as practicable, and, except to positions which are policy-determining, primarily confidential, or highly technical, by competitive examination.' GOCCs with original charters are part of the civil service under Sec. 2(1), so they are not an exception.

items.q: During the campaign period, Mr. Dela Paz, a records officer in a municipal assessor's office, handed out campaign flyers for a mayoral candidate to clients of the office. Which constitutional rule on the civil service did he violate?
choices: No officer or employee of the civil service shall engage, directly or indirectly, in any electioneering or partisan political campaign
No public officer shall receive additional, double, or indirect compensation
Appointments shall be made only according to merit and fitness
Congress shall provide for the standardization of compensation
items.why: Art. IX-B, Sec. 2(4) states: 'No officer or employee in the civil service shall engage, directly or indirectly, in any electioneering or partisan political campaign.' The other choices are real rules (Sec. 8, Sec. 2(2), Sec. 5) but have nothing to do with campaigning.

items.q: Rolando ran for municipal councilor and lost. Two months after the election, the mayor wants to appoint him as head of a municipal office. What does the 1987 Constitution provide?
choices: He may be appointed at once because he holds no elective office
He may be appointed only to a primarily confidential position
He cannot be appointed to any office in the Government within one year after the election
He may be appointed if the Civil Service Commission approves
items.why: Art. IX-B, Sec. 6: 'No candidate who has lost in any election, shall within one year after such election, be appointed to any office in the Government or any Government-owned or controlled corporations or in any of their subsidiaries.' The rule has no exception for confidential positions or CSC approval.

items.q: Under the common provisions on the Constitutional Commissions, within what period must each Commission decide a case submitted to it, and within what period may an aggrieved party bring the decision to the Supreme Court on certiorari?
choices: 30 days to decide; 15 days from receipt of a copy of the decision
60 days to decide; 30 days from receipt of a copy of the decision
90 days to decide; 60 days from receipt of a copy of the decision
120 days to decide; 30 days from promulgation
items.why: Art. IX-A, Sec. 7: each Commission decides by a majority vote of all its Members 'within sixty days from the date of its submission for decision or resolution', and, unless otherwise provided by the Constitution or by law, its decision 'may be brought to the Supreme Court on certiorari by the aggrieved party within thirty days from receipt of a copy thereof.'

items.q: What power does the President exercise over local governments under Art. X, Sec. 4 of the 1987 Constitution?
choices: No power at all, because of local autonomy
items.why: Art. X, Sec. 4 states: 'The President of the Philippines shall exercise general supervision over local governments.' Control is the power the President has over 'all the executive departments, bureaus, and offices' under Art. VII, Sec. 17, which is the common trap.

items.q: Which of the following officials may be removed from office by impeachment under Art. XI, Sec. 2?
choices: A Secretary of an executive department
items.why: Art. XI, Sec. 2 names 'The President, the Vice-President, the Members of the Supreme Court, the Members of the Constitutional Commissions, and the Ombudsman' as impeachable, and adds that 'All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, but not by impeachment.' Cabinet secretaries, Senators and governors are not on the list.

items.q: Under Art. XVII, Sec. 2, amendments to the Constitution may be directly proposed by the people through initiative upon a petition signed by at least how many registered voters?
choices: 10% of the total registered voters, with every legislative district represented by at least 3%
12% of the total registered voters, with every legislative district represented by at least 3%
12% of the total registered voters, with every province represented by at least 5%
25% of the total registered voters nationwide
items.why: Art. XVII, Sec. 2 requires 'a petition of at least twelve per centum of the total number of registered voters, of which every legislative district must be represented by at least three per centum of the registered voters therein.' The 10% and 3% figures belong to initiative and referendum on laws (Art. VI, Sec. 32).

items.q: Under R.A. 6713, within how many working days from receipt must a public official or employee respond to letters, telegrams or other communications sent by the public?
items.why: Sec. 5(a) requires officials and employees, 'within fifteen (15) working days from receipt thereof, [to] respond to letters, telegrams or other means of communications sent by the public. The reply must contain the action taken on the request.' Ten working days is the period after which filed SALNs become available for copying (Sec. 8(C)(2)).

items.q: Nestor, a government accountant, drives an ordinary car, avoids showing off expensive gadgets or jewelry, and keeps a lifestyle that fits his salary. Which norm of conduct under R.A. 6713 does he best show?
items.why: Sec. 4(A)(h), Simple living: officials and employees and their families 'shall lead modest lives appropriate to their positions and income. They shall not indulge in extravagant or ostentatious display of wealth in any form.' Professionalism is about excellence and skill in performing duties, not lifestyle.

items.q: A clerk at the city treasurer's office serves a taxpayer as promptly as everyone else, even though the taxpayer is a known supporter of the party opposing the mayor. Which norm of conduct under R.A. 6713 is the clerk observing?
items.why: Sec. 4(A)(d), Political neutrality: officials and employees 'shall provide service to everyone without unfair discrimination and regardless of party affiliation or preference.' Commitment to democracy (Sec. 4(A)(g)) is about democratic values and civilian supremacy, not equal service across party lines.

items.q: Under the norm of justness and sincerity in R.A. 6713, public officials shall not extend undue favors on account of their office to their relatives. What exception does the law itself state?
choices: Appointment of relatives to positions in other government agencies
Granting relatives priority in the processing of permits
Hiring relatives as consultants if they are qualified
Appointment of relatives to positions considered strictly confidential or as members of their personal staff whose terms are coterminous with theirs
items.why: Sec. 4(A)(c) says officials 'shall not dispense or extend undue favors on account of their office to their relatives whether by consanguinity or affinity except with respect to appointments of such relatives to positions considered strictly confidential or as members of their personal staff whose terms are coterminous with theirs.' Being qualified is not the stated exception.

items.q: As defined in R.A. 6713, "relatives" of a public official or employee are persons related to him or her within what degree?
choices: Second civil degree of consanguinity only
Third civil degree of consanguinity or affinity
Fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity
Fifth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity
items.why: Sec. 3(k): 'Relatives' refers to 'any and all persons related to a public official or employee within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity, including bilas, inso and balae.' Do not confuse this with 'family' in Sec. 3(g), which means only the spouse and unmarried children under 18.

items.q: Ella resigned as an inspector of a government office that licenses private security agencies. Under Sec. 7(b) of R.A. 6713, when may she accept a job as manager of a security agency licensed by her former office?
choices: Immediately after her resignation takes effect
Only after one year from her resignation
Only after three years from her resignation
Never, because the prohibition is permanent
items.why: Sec. 7(b)(1) bars officials from managing or being employed by a private enterprise 'regulated, supervised or licensed by their office', and the same subsection says these prohibitions 'shall continue to apply for a period of one (1) year after resignation, retirement, or separation from public office.' The bar is neither immediate release nor permanent.

items.q: As to gifts or grants from foreign governments, R.A. 6713 states that Congress consents to the acceptance by a public official or employee of which of the following?
choices: A gift in the nature of a scholarship or fellowship grant or medical treatment
Cash of any amount given during an official visit
A car given as a token of friendship
Free shares of stock in a foreign company
items.why: Sec. 7(d) lists what Congress consents to: (i) a gift of nominal value received 'as a souvenir or mark of courtesy'; (ii) 'a gift in the nature of a scholarship or fellowship grant or medical treatment'; and (iii) certain travel grants for travel entirely outside the Philippines if permitted by the head of office. Cash, cars and shares are not on the list.

items.q: Under the definition of "gift" in R.A. 6713, which of the following is NOT considered a gift?
choices: A car sold to an official through a simulated sale
A free trip given in exchange for a favorable decision
Expensive jewelry given at Christmas by a contractor with a pending bid
An unsolicited gift of nominal or insignificant value not given in anticipation of, or in exchange for, a favor
items.why: Sec. 3(c) defines a gift to include 'a simulated sale or an ostensibly onerous disposition thereof' but says it 'shall not include an unsolicited gift of nominal or insignificant value not given in anticipation of, or in exchange for, a favor'. Sec. 3(d) adds that a valuable gift is covered 'even on the occasion of a family celebration or national festivity like Christmas'.

items.q: Under R.A. 6713, after the first filing upon assumption of office, by what date every year must the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) be filed?
items.why: Sec. 8(A) says the documents must be filed '(a) within thirty (30) days after assumption of office; (b) on or before April 30, of every year thereafter; and (c) within thirty (30) days after separation from the service.'

items.q: A new appointee sits on the board of, and owns shares in, a private company whose interests may be affected by his official duties. Under Sec. 9 of R.A. 6713, what must he do?
choices: Resign from the board within 30 days from assumption of office and divest his shares within 60 days from assumption
Resign from the board within 60 days and divest his shares within 90 days
Declare the interest in his SALN; no resignation or divestment is needed
Transfer the shares to his spouse within 30 days
items.why: Sec. 9: 'When a conflict of interest arises, he shall resign from his position in any private business enterprise within thirty (30) days from his assumption of office and/or divest himself of his shareholdings or interest within sixty (60) days from such assumption.' A transfer to a spouse is not divestment, since Sec. 3(j) requires a transfer to persons 'other than his spouse and relatives'.

items.q: Under Sec. 11(a) of R.A. 6713, which administrative penalties may be imposed on a public official or employee who violates the Act, depending on the gravity of the offense and after due notice and hearing?
choices: A fine not exceeding one month's salary or a reprimand only
A fine not exceeding six months' salary, suspension not exceeding one year, or removal
Suspension not exceeding six months only
items.why: Sec. 11(a): a violator 'shall be punished with a fine not exceeding the equivalent of six (6) months' salary or suspension not exceeding one (1) year, or removal depending on the gravity of the offense after due notice and hearing by the appropriate body or agency.' Due notice and hearing are always required.

items.q: Which agency has the primary responsibility for the administration and enforcement of R.A. 6713?
items.why: Sec. 12: 'The Civil Service Commission shall have the primary responsibility for the administration and enforcement of this Act.' The Ombudsman has specific roles in the law (for example, regulations on foreign gifts under Sec. 7(d) and protecting citizens who report violations), but not the primary responsibility.

items.q: According to Art. II, Sec. 2 of the 1987 Constitution, the Philippines renounces war as:
choices: a means of settling disputes with non-allied states only
a last resort that needs United Nations approval
a matter to be decided by the President alone
items.why: Art. II, Sec. 2: 'The Philippines renounces war as an instrument of national policy, adopts the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the land and adheres to the policy of peace, equality, justice, freedom, cooperation, and amity with all nations.'

items.q: Which of the following is a power of the Commission on Human Rights under Art. XIII, Sec. 18 of the 1987 Constitution?
choices: To try and decide criminal cases involving human rights violations
To issue warrants of arrest against suspected violators
To dismiss erring police officers from the service
To exercise visitorial powers over jails, prisons, or detention facilities
items.why: Art. XIII, Sec. 18(4) empowers the CHR to 'Exercise visitorial powers over jails, prisons, or detention facilities.' Its other powers include investigating 'all forms of human rights violations involving civil and political rights' and recommending measures to Congress. It investigates and recommends; it does not try cases, issue arrest warrants, or dismiss officials.

items.q: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was proclaimed by which body, and in what year?
choices: The United Nations Human Rights Council, 1966
items.why: The United Nations text of the UDHR states that the Declaration 'was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations.' Its Article 1 begins: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'
